title: Liveness probe
text: A liveness probe tells the kubelet whether a container is still healthy. If the probe fails more than failureThreshold times in a row, the kubelet kills the container and the restart policy decides what happens next. Liveness probes do not affect whether a Pod receives traffic; they only decide whether the container is restarted.

title: Readiness probe
text: A readiness probe tells Kubernetes whether a container can accept requests. While the probe fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints and receives no traffic, but the container is not restarted. Readiness is the right probe for temporary conditions such as warming a cache or waiting for a downstream dependency.

title: Startup probe
text: A startup probe protects slow-starting containers. Until it succeeds, liveness and readiness probes are disabled, so a container that needs several minutes to boot is not killed prematurely. The total budget is periodSeconds multiplied by failureThreshold; a database migration on first boot is a typical reason to widen it.

title: Resource requests and limits
text: A resource request is what the scheduler reserves for a container on a node; a limit is the ceiling enforced at runtime. A container that exceeds its memory limit is OOM-killed, while exceeding a CPU limit only throttles it. Requests decide placement, limits decide enforcement.

title: OOMKilled containers
text: When a container's memory usage crosses its limit, the kernel's OOM killer terminates the process and the Pod shows a last state of OOMKilled with exit code 137. The fix is either to raise the memory limit or to reduce the workload's footprint; restarting the Pod alone does not address the cause.

title: CrashLoopBackOff
text: CrashLoopBackOff means a container keeps exiting and the kubelet is waiting an increasing back-off interval before the next restart. The status is a symptom, not a cause: the previous container's logs, fetched with the --previous flag, and the exit code usually reveal why the process is dying.

title: Pods stuck in Pending
text: A Pod stays Pending when the scheduler cannot place it. Common reasons are insufficient CPU or memory on any node, an unsatisfiable node selector or affinity rule, a taint without a matching toleration, or a PersistentVolumeClaim that has not been bound. The Events section of kubectl describe names the exact reason.

title: Services and EndpointSlices
text: A Service selects Pods by label and publishes their addresses as EndpointSlices. If a Service has no endpoints, the selector does not match any ready Pod: either the labels differ or the Pods are failing their readiness probe. Traffic to a Service with empty endpoints is refused.

title: Ingress versus Gateway API
text: Ingress is the older Kubernetes API for HTTP routing, with behaviour that varies between controllers and relies heavily on annotations. Gateway API replaces it with typed resources: GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute and ReferenceGrant. It separates infrastructure ownership from application routing and is the direction new controllers take.

title: ReferenceGrant
text: A ReferenceGrant allows a resource in one namespace to reference a resource in another. An HTTPRoute in namespace app that points at a Gateway in namespace gateway-system needs a ReferenceGrant in the target namespace, or the reference is rejected and the route never becomes accepted.

title: HTTPRoute
text: An HTTPRoute attaches to a Gateway through parentRefs and describes matching rules and backends. A rule can match on path prefix, headers or method and send traffic to one or more Services by name and port. Several routes from different namespaces can share one Gateway listener.

title: NetworkPolicy
text: A NetworkPolicy restricts which Pods can talk to each other at layer 3 and 4. Policies are additive: once any policy selects a Pod, all traffic not explicitly allowed is denied in that direction. Enforcement depends on the CNI plugin; a cluster whose CNI ignores policies silently allows everything.

title: ConfigMap and Secret
text: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration and Secrets hold credentials, both consumed as environment variables or mounted files. Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted, unless encryption at rest is enabled on the API server. Mounted files update when the object changes; environment variables do not.

title: RBAC roles and bindings
text: RBAC grants permissions through Roles and ClusterRoles, which list verbs on resources, and through RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings, which attach those rules to users, groups or service accounts. A Role is namespaced; a ClusterRole applies cluster-wide or can be bound inside a single namespace.

title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
text: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the replica count of a Deployment based on observed metrics such as CPU utilisation or a custom metric. It needs resource requests to compute utilisation percentages and it scales between minReplicas and maxReplicas with a stabilisation window to avoid flapping.

title: KinD clusters
text: KinD runs a Kubernetes cluster inside Docker containers, one container per node. It is meant for local development and CI rather than production. Because the nodes are containers on a Docker bridge network, image pulls from inside the cluster depend on the host's Docker egress rules.

title: Flux OCIRepository
text: An OCIRepository is a Flux source that points at an OCI artifact in a registry and tracks a tag, semver range or digest. The source-controller downloads the artifact and exposes it for Kustomizations and HelmReleases. It is the building block for GitOps without a Git server, where CI pushes manifests as artifacts.

title: Flux GitRepository
text: A GitRepository is a Flux source that clones a Git repository at a branch, tag or commit and packages the checkout as an artifact. An ignore field with gitignore syntax limits which paths land in the artifact. Changing the ignore rules does not by itself produce a new artifact if the revision is unchanged.

title: Flux HelmRepository
text: A HelmRepository is a Flux source for a classic Helm chart index served over HTTP. The HelmRelease references it through chart.spec.sourceRef and picks a chart name and version. For charts published as OCI artifacts, an OCIRepository with chartRef is used instead.

title: Flux Kustomization
text: A Flux Kustomization applies a path from a source artifact to the cluster on an interval. With prune enabled, objects removed from the source are deleted from the cluster. With wait enabled, the Kustomization is not marked Ready until every applied object reports healthy, which makes dependsOn between Kustomizations meaningful.

title: Flux HelmRelease
text: A HelmRelease is Flux's declarative wrapper around a Helm release: chart reference, values, install and upgrade strategy. Values live inline or come from ConfigMaps and Secrets. A postRenderers section can patch rendered manifests with Kustomize before they are applied, which is the way to fix a chart you cannot change.

title: Flux dependsOn
text: dependsOn orders reconciliation between Flux objects of the same kind. A HelmRelease that installs custom resources must depend on the HelmRelease that installs the matching CRDs, or it fails with no matches for kind until the next retry. Flux does not infer this ordering from the manifests.

title: Semver build metadata in Helm labels
text: Flux appends the artifact digest to a chart version as semver build metadata, producing a version such as 1.2.3+abcdef. Charts that copy the chart version into app.kubernetes.io/version or into an image tag then fail, because the plus sign is not a valid label value or image tag character. The fix is to set those values explicitly.

title: CRD lifecycle in Helm charts
text: Helm installs CRDs from a chart's crds directory on first install but never upgrades them. Flux's HelmRelease can be told to create or replace CRDs on upgrade through the install and upgrade crds policy. Keeping CRDs in a separate chart and release makes the ordering explicit and the upgrade path predictable.

title: Terraform state
text: Terraform state maps resources in configuration to real objects and stores attributes the provider returned. Local state is a file on disk; a remote backend such as S3 with locking is required when more than one person or pipeline applies. Losing state does not destroy infrastructure, but it makes Terraform forget it exists.

title: Plan before apply
text: terraform plan computes the difference between configuration and state and prints the actions that apply would take. Reviewing the plan is where resource replacements are caught: a change marked with a minus and plus sign destroys and recreates the object, which for a database or a cluster means downtime and possibly data loss.

title: Import and moved blocks
text: An import block or terraform import brings an existing object under Terraform management without recreating it. A moved block renames a resource address in state so refactoring modules does not produce a destroy and create. Both are ways of editing state declaratively instead of by hand.

title: Configuration drift
text: Drift is a difference between the real object and Terraform state caused by changes made outside Terraform, such as a manual edit in a console. The next plan shows the difference and apply reverts it, which can surprise whoever made the manual change. Refreshing state records the drift without undoing it.

title: Provider lock file
text: The .terraform.lock.hcl file pins the exact provider versions and checksums selected during init. Committing it makes every machine and pipeline use the same provider builds. Upgrading a provider is a deliberate init with the upgrade flag, followed by a plan review.

title: OpenTofu
text: OpenTofu is an open-source fork of Terraform maintained under the Linux Foundation after the licence change. It reads the same configuration language and state format, and the CLI is invoked as tofu instead of terraform. Some features, such as write-only attributes, appeared in OpenTofu before or independently of Terraform.

title: 502 Bad Gateway in NGINX
text: NGINX returns 502 when it could not get a valid response from the upstream: the connection was refused, reset or returned garbage. The error log names the upstream address and the reason. Check that the upstream process listens on the configured address and port before touching timeouts or buffers.

title: 504 Gateway Timeout in NGINX
text: NGINX returns 504 when the upstream accepted the connection but did not answer within proxy_read_timeout. The upstream is alive but slow. Raising the timeout hides the symptom; the durable fix is on the application side, unless the request is legitimately long-running.

title: 413 Request Entity Too Large
text: NGINX rejects a request body larger than client_max_body_size with 413. The default is one megabyte, which breaks file uploads. The directive can be set in http, server or location context, and the closest context wins.

title: Reload versus restart
text: nginx -s reload, or systemctl reload, starts new worker processes with the new configuration and lets the old workers finish their connections, so no requests are dropped. A restart kills workers immediately. Always run nginx -t first, because a reload with a broken configuration is refused and the old configuration stays active.

title: Client IP behind a load balancer
text: Behind a proxy or load balancer, NGINX sees the proxy's address as the client. The real_ip module replaces it with the value from X-Forwarded-For when the connection comes from an address listed in set_real_ip_from. Without that list, anyone can spoof the header.

title: ALB target health checks
text: An Application Load Balancer only sends traffic to targets whose health check passes. A target shows unhealthy when the check path returns a status outside the configured matcher, when the security group blocks the load balancer's subnet, or when the instance or Pod is not listening. The target group's health status names the failure reason.

title: Security groups versus network ACLs
text: A security group is a stateful firewall attached to a network interface: allowed inbound traffic is automatically allowed back out. A network ACL is a stateless filter on a subnet with ordered allow and deny rules, so return traffic on ephemeral ports must be allowed explicitly. Most connectivity problems are security groups, not ACLs.

title: IAM policy evaluation
text: IAM evaluates every request against all applicable policies. An explicit Deny anywhere wins over any Allow; without an explicit Allow the default is Deny. Permission boundaries and service control policies cap what identity policies can grant, which is why an Allow in a role can still be denied.

title: IAM roles for service accounts
text: IAM roles for service accounts let a Pod on EKS assume an IAM role through a projected service account token and an OIDC provider, instead of sharing the node's instance profile. The role's trust policy names the cluster's OIDC issuer and the service account. Pod Identity is the newer alternative that avoids the OIDC setup.

title: OpenTelemetry Collector
text: The OpenTelemetry Collector receives traces, metrics and logs over OTLP, processes them in a pipeline and exports them to one or more backends. Running it as a gateway between applications and the backend decouples instrumentation from the vendor. A missing exporter or a wrong OTLP endpoint is the usual reason spans never arrive.

title: CloudWatch alarm states
text: A CloudWatch alarm evaluates a metric over a period and enters ALARM when the threshold is crossed for the configured number of datapoints. INSUFFICIENT_DATA means no datapoints arrived, which for a metric that only reports on error may be healthy. Treat missing data explicitly with the missing data setting instead of assuming it is a failure.

title: Matryoshka embeddings
text: Matryoshka Representation Learning trains an embedding model so that the first N dimensions of a vector are themselves a usable embedding. A 768-dimensional vector can be truncated to 256 and re-normalised with a small loss in retrieval quality, which cuts index size and search cost. The model must be trained this way; truncating an ordinary embedding destroys it.

title: Cosine similarity
text: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ignores their length. For unit-length vectors it equals the dot product, which is why embedding models normalise their output and why a truncated Matryoshka vector must be normalised again. Scores range from minus one to one, with one meaning identical direction.

title: Chunking for retrieval
text: Documents are split into chunks before embedding because a single vector cannot represent a long document well and because the retrieved unit must fit in the model's context. Splitting on natural boundaries such as headings, YAML documents or code blocks keeps a chunk self-contained. Overly small chunks lose context; overly large ones dilute the signal.

title: Query and document prefixes
text: Many embedding models are trained with a task prefix that distinguishes queries from documents, such as search_query and search_document, or an instruction line on the query side. Omitting the prefix the model was trained with measurably lowers retrieval quality. The prefix convention is model-specific and must be applied consistently at indexing and query time.
